history.heading: Early Estonia and crusaders
paragraphs: Finnic peoples, ancestors of the Estonians, have lived on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea for thousands of years. In the 13th century, during the Northern Crusades, German and Danish knights conquered the region. Tallinn and other towns joined the Hanseatic League, and a Baltic German nobility dominated the land, while Estonians were mostly peasant serfs.
Tallinn's Old Town, one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Northern Europe, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: Swedish and Russian rule
paragraphs: Estonia came under Swedish rule in the 16th and 17th centuries, a period remembered for founding schools and the University of Tartu (1632). After the Great Northern War, Russia took control in 1710. Serfdom was abolished in the early 19th century, and a national awakening followed, with song festivals beginning in 1869.

history.heading: Independence and occupation
paragraphs: Estonia declared independence on 24 February 1918 and defended it in the War of Independence against Soviet Russia. Under the 1939 Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union occupied Estonia in 1940. Mass deportations to Siberia followed, then Nazi German occupation and Soviet reoccupation in 1944. Tens of thousands fled to the West.

Under Soviet rule, large-scale Russian-speaking immigration changed the population. In the late 1980s, the "Singing Revolution" of peaceful mass song gatherings led to restored independence on 20 August 1991.

history.heading: Modern Estonia
paragraphs: Estonia carried out rapid market reforms, joined NATO and the European Union in 2004, and adopted the euro in 2011. It became known as one of the world's most digitally advanced societies.

culture.heading: Language and song
paragraphs: Estonian is a Finno-Ugric language closely related to Finnish. About a quarter of the population is ethnically Russian, mostly in Tallinn and the northeast. Estonia is one of the least religious countries in the world.
The Song Festival, held every five years with tens of thousands of singers, is a central part of identity and recognised by UNESCO. Composer Arvo Pärt is one of the most performed living composers.

culture.heading: Nature and traditions
paragraphs: Forests cover about half of the country, and saunas, especially the smoke saunas of Võromaa, are part of daily life. Midsummer (Jaanipäev) is celebrated with bonfires. Food includes black rye bread, kama, and herring.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Estonia is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Riigikogu (parliament), while the president, elected by parliament or an electoral college, is head of state.

Estonia pioneered online voting in national elections and digital public services. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, security and defence have dominated politics; Estonia is one of the largest supporters of Ukraine relative to its economy.

economy.heading: A digital economy
paragraphs: Estonia has a high-income economy with a strong technology sector. It has produced several "unicorn" startups, including Skype, Wise and Bolt, and offers e-residency to entrepreneurs worldwide.

Other key sectors include manufacturing, timber and wood products, logistics and services. Estonia has a simple tax system and low public debt. The currency is the euro. Oil shale was long used for energy, and the country is transitioning to renewables.
